cover.headline: From a Single Question to 542 Temples
cover.dek: Three months after the first domain was registered, PuniCodex restores the original names of myth, place, and sacred tradition across twenty-five pantheons — and invites the world inside.
body: On 25 May 2026 a single question was written into a registrar search box: *why do the gods live in ASCII?* The names that had shaped human imagination for millennia — Apóllōn, Hekátē, Śakti, Tōnatiuh — were reduced to plain Latin letters in the digital realm, stripped of stress, length, script, and soul. PuniCodex began as an attempt to give those names back their original Unicode form.

By 1 September that attempt has become 542 flagship temples. Each one is a complete scholarly edition: restored orthography, original script or transliteration, a rules-derived pronunciation, mythology, archaeology, a curated gallery, industry-pattern mappings, a blog, and a scholars tab edited under university sponsorship. The project now spans twenty-five pantheons, from the Olympians to the Aboriginal Dreamtime, and holds 980 lexicon entries across the restored traditions.

This first edition of *The Unicode Herald* records that transformation. It introduces the new per-pantheon pages and the movie guide, explains how sponsorship and patronage keep the lore free of intrusive advertising, and sets out the goals for the next quarter: hardening the automated sponsorship pipeline, expanding university collaboration, and preparing the Reliquary store and Mythic Duel card game for wider release.

landing.tagline: The quarterly encyclopedia of the Unicode Pantheon
landing.blurb: Every quarter, *The Unicode Herald* publishes a deep-dive edition covering temple news, scholarly features, sponsorship openings, and the project's roadmap. The inaugural issue charts the first three months of PuniCodex — from a single domain registration to 542 flagship temples.

chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.subtitle: The question that started the pantheon
body: PuniCodex began with a simple observation: the internet speaks ASCII, but the names of the gods never did. The project set out to restore those names — with their stress marks, length marks, original scripts, and scholarly transliterations — as first-class digital citizens.

What started as a registrar search on 25 May 2026 has grown into 542 flagship temples across twenty-five pantheons. Each temple is both a scholarly edition and a marketplace of meaning: a place where ancient names meet modern sponsorship, student creativity, and respectful commerce.

This inaugural issue of *The Unicode Herald* is a snapshot of that growth. It is also a promise: the pantheon will keep expanding, the scholarship will keep deepening, and the doors will stay open to anyone who believes the original names matter.

sections.title: The Fleet
sections.body: The pantheon now holds 980 lexicon entries, 542 built flagship temples, 25 distinct pantheons, and 352 owned Unicode domains. The newest traditions to receive full flagship treatment are Aboriginal, Baltic, Hittite, Korean, Mapuche, and Slavic.

sections.title: Ninety Days of Attention
sections.body: Human readers spent an average of 3 minutes 6 seconds per session across 20,955 unique sessions. Bot traffic accounted for 14.2% of raw requests; 3,231 bot views were filtered out so the analytics reflect genuine human interest.

sections.title: Trending This Week
sections.body: Jagannātha leads the past seven days with 76 human views, followed by Vǫr, Auðhumla, Epimētheús, and Vár. The trending board resets monthly and is surfaced on the /trending/ page.

chapters.title: New This Quarter
chapters.subtitle: Screen guide, pantheon pages, and domainless flagships

sections.title: Per-Pantheon Landing Pages
sections.body: Twenty-five dedicated pages now open the major traditions — [/greek/](/greek/), [/norse/](/norse/), [/egyptian/](/egyptian/), [/sanskrit/](/sanskrit/), [/japanese/](/japanese/), and twenty more. Each page tells the cultural story of the pantheon, links to its sacred texts where they exist, and displays every flagship temple in that tradition as a browsable grid. Built for discovery and for search engines alike.

sections.title: The Screen Guide
sections.body: A new [/screen/](/screen/) guide maps films, series, and games that feature mythological characters back to their temples. From *Percy Jackson and the Olympians* to *Princess Mononoke*, *God of War Ragnarök* to *Record of Ragnarok*, each entry explains what the production got right, where it took liberties, and which temples to visit for the scholarly source.

sections.title: Domainless Flagships
sections.body: Many names central to world mythology — Susanō, Helénē, Rāvaṇa, Óneiros — already own their .com homes. Many others do not. A new class of flagship temple now exists for unregisterable or taken ASCII names, created with the same scholarly depth as owned temples but without claiming a domain. These expand the pantheon's coverage without diluting its integrity.

chapters.title: Sponsors & Patrons
chapters.subtitle: How the temples stay free of intrusive advertising
body: Every flagship temple offers thirteen sponsorship frames — crown banner, column frames, inline placements, ribbon, seal, inscription, emblem, sigil, crest, and keystone. Each placement is reviewed by hand for quality and relevance to the temple's tradition. Sponsors receive live analytics, quarterly written reports, and alignment across kindred temples.

Patron subscriptions offer a lighter way to support a temple: a recurring contribution that places the patron's name or brand beside the deity's lore and links to their social or professional profiles.

Importantly, sponsorship and patronage live on their own pages and frames. They never interrupt the lore, the scholarly text, or the reading experience. The model connects the modern world to mythology while preserving respect for the content it supports.

chapters.title: University Collaboration
chapters.subtitle: Removing the fee, opening the door
body: The Scholarly Edition is edited under university sponsorship. For Q4 2026 PuniCodex is moving away from the $999-per-year institutional fee and toward a barter model: universities provide curation, student contributors, and a cross-link from their humanities or history department; PuniCodex displays their logo on the academic collaborators strip and gives their students free access to technological, scholarly, and utility features.

The goal is to align the project's growth with free educational value. Student contributors gain portfolio work in digital humanities, sponsors gain a vetted creative pipeline, and the pantheon gains peer-reviewed depth.

chapters.title: The Reliquary
chapters.subtitle: Print-on-demand and the physical pantheon
body: The Reliquary is the print-on-demand arm of the project. Every flagship temple now has thirteen product types — tee, hoodie, crewneck, cap, mug, tumbler, tote, phone case, notebook, sticker, pin, print, and canvas — plus an eight-item house line. Products are produced on demand through Printful, keeping inventory risk low while offering physical artifacts tied to the temples.

Next quarter the store pipeline will be connected to Google Merchant Center and strengthened with mockup automation, variant pricing, and marketing collateral so the temples can reach buyers beyond the site itself.

chapters.title: Mythic Duel & Cards
chapters.subtitle: The game under construction
body: The First Restoration card set and the Mythic Duel engine remain under active construction. Every flagship temple prints common, rare, legendary, and mythic editions; domainless flagships enter as archive printings and can climb on promotion. The deterministic duel engine uses seeded RNG so matches are replayable and fair.

In August the card work took a deliberate back seat so the pantheon expansion could reach 542 temples. With that milestone reached, the next quarter returns focus to pack logic, ink economy, card renderer polish, and mobile play.

sections.title: Sponsorship Automation
sections.body: Harden the admin portal, creative review, and advertiser panel until the full booking flow is enterprise-grade and self-service.

sections.title: Marketing Outreach
sections.body: Launch targeted outreach for business sponsorship with the new per-temple pages, analytics, and Herald profiles as proof points.

sections.title: Oracle & API
sections.body: Expand the Oracle question-answering layer and publish richer API documentation for researchers and integrators.

sections.title: Cross-Temple Patronage
sections.body: Build a feature that lets a single sponsor or patron appear across multiple related temples, broadening visibility while keeping placements relevant.

chapters.title: Colophon
chapters.subtitle: Credits and print note
body: *The Unicode Herald* is the quarterly publication of the Unicode Pantheon, published by PuniCodex in virtual and physical editions. Temple content is drawn from the project's Scholarly Edition and peer-reviewed under university sponsorship. Analytics are bot-filtered and reflect human engagement across the pantheon.
